title: Subsets
directAnswer: Return the power set — every subset of a distinct-element array. The canonical answer is backtracking with a start index where you record the path at EVERY node (not just leaves), because every partial path is itself a valid subset. Choose `nums[i]`, recurse with `i + 1` (each element used at most once), then un-choose. There are exactly 2ⁿ subsets, so any correct solution is O(2ⁿ).

remember.pattern: Backtracking with a start index, recording every node (choose → explore → un-choose)
rules: Record the path at **every** node, not only at the leaves — unlike Combination Sum, there's no target to hit; every partial path is a valid subset.
Recurse with `i + 1` (not `i`) so each element is used **at most once** — passing `i` would allow reuse and produce multisets.
Loop from `start`, never `0` — the **never-go-backward** rule emits subsets in index order and prevents duplicates like {1,2} and {2,1}.
Append a **copy** `path[:]` — the live list is mutated by later pops and would corrupt every stored subset.
There are exactly **2ⁿ** subsets including the empty set and the full set — any solution is `O(2ⁿ)`; you can't beat the output size.
whenToUse: Asked to enumerate **all** subsets / the power set of distinct elements
Need every combination of choices where each element is independently in or out
The result must include the empty set and the full set
Search space is a binary in/out decision per element
antiSignals: Only the **count** of subsets is needed → it's just 2ⁿ, no enumeration required
Input has duplicates and you must dedup → Subsets II (sort + skip same-level repeats)
Need subsets of a fixed size k only → Combinations (LC 77), prune by length
n is large (> ~20) → 2ⁿ is intractable; the problem likely wants DP or math, not enumeration
remember.takeaway: Subsets is the purest backtracking template: a binary include/exclude choice per element with no constraint to satisfy. The 'record at every node' twist distinguishes it from constraint problems like Combination Sum. Master it and Subsets II, Combinations, and Permutations are one-line variations.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that every node of the recursion tree is a valid subset (so you record everywhere, not just at leaves), and whether you control the start index to avoid duplicates. Bonus: knowing the bitmask alternative and that 2ⁿ is a hard lower bound.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Only recording at the leaves (giving subsets of one fixed size instead of all), passing `i` instead of `i + 1` (allowing reuse), or storing the live `path` reference so all results mutate to the same list.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that the answer size is exactly 2ⁿ so O(2ⁿ) is optimal, show the choose/explore/un-choose recursion, then offer the bitmask iterative version as a clean O(2ⁿ · n) alternative with no recursion stack.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` of **unique** elements, return **all possible subsets** (the power set).

The solution set **must not contain duplicate subsets**. Return the solution in any order.
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique
understanding: Produce the power set: every possible selection of elements, from the empty set up to the whole array. Because every element is either in or out independently, there are 2ⁿ subsets. Elements are unique, so we never have to worry about duplicate subsets arising from equal values — only from revisiting the same element in different order, which the start index prevents.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the elements unique, or can there be duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Unique. That's important — duplicates would require an extra dedup step (sort + skip same-level repeats), which is Subsets II (LC 90).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should the empty subset and the full array be included?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the power set includes both the empty set [] and the complete array. That's why we record at every node, including the root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of subsets (or of elements within a subset) matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Any order is accepted. We still emit each subset once; the start index guarantees we never produce {1,2} and {2,1} as separate answers.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most 10, so 2¹⁰ = 1024 subsets — tiny. Exponential enumeration is comfortably fast; the constraint is a hint that brute-force enumeration is intended.

examples.explanation: All 2³ = 8 subsets. Order doesn't matter; this is the order the start-index backtracking produces.
Two subsets: the empty set and {0}. Note 0 is a valid element — don't let it trip up any truthiness checks.
4 subsets. {2,1} never appears separately because the loop only moves forward from start.

approaches.name: Backtracking with Start Index (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Phrase it as 'binary in/out choice per element — record the path at every node, recurse with i+1 so each element is used once'.
hints: There are 2ⁿ subsets because each element is independently in or out. Can you grow a subset one element at a time, branching on 'take this element' vs 'skip it'?
Use a `start` index and loop `i` from `start`. 'Choose' nums[i] (append), recurse from `i + 1`, then 'un-choose' (pop). What's different from Combination Sum is when you record an answer.
Unlike a sum-target problem, there's no condition to wait for — every partial path is already a valid subset. So record the path at the TOP of every call, before the loop.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2ⁿ subsets and the recursion visits exactly 2ⁿ nodes (one per subset). At each node we copy the path, which costs up to O(n). So total work is O(n · 2ⁿ) time. Excluding the output, extra space is just the recursion depth and the live path, both O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Grow a subset one element at a time. At each call, first **record** the current path (it's a complete, valid subset on its own), then loop `i` from `start` to the end: **choose** `nums[i]` by appending it, **explore** by recursing from `i + 1`, then **un-choose** by popping it. The recursion bottoms out naturally when the loop has no more elements to add.

**Why we record at every node, not just at leaves.** This is the one idea that separates Subsets from constraint problems like Combination Sum. There, an answer is only valid when the running sum hits the target, so you record only at qualifying leaves. Here there is *no* constraint — the empty set, every singleton, every pair, and the full array are all legitimate subsets. Each node of the recursion tree corresponds to exactly one subset (the elements chosen on the path from the root), so recording at the top of every call captures all 2ⁿ of them, including the empty set at the root.

**Why recurse with `i + 1` and not `i`.** Passing `i + 1` means the next level can only consider elements *after* the one we just picked, so each element is used **at most once** — which is what makes these subsets rather than multisets. If you passed `i` (as Combination Sum does for reuse), you'd generate [1,1], [1,1,1], and so on. The single-character difference between `i` and `i + 1` is the lever that flips 'reuse allowed' to 'each element once' — name it explicitly in the interview.

**Why the loop starts at `start`, never 0.** Starting at `start` enforces that subsets are always built in increasing index order, so we generate {1,2} but never {2,1}. Without it, the same subset would appear in multiple orderings and the result would contain duplicates. Combined with `i + 1`, the start index guarantees each subset is produced exactly once.

**Why the un-choose (pop) and the copy both matter.** `path` is a single shared list threaded through the entire tree. After exploring the branch that picked `nums[i]`, we `pop()` it so the next sibling iteration starts from the correct prefix — skip the pop and choices bleed across branches. And when we record, we append `path[:]` (a snapshot); appending the live `path` stores a reference that subsequent pops mutate, leaving every stored subset corrupted.
approaches.insight: Subsets is the degenerate case of the backtracking family where the 'constraint' is trivially always satisfied. That's why you record at every node instead of only at qualifying leaves. Once you see subsets as 'a binary in/out decision per element', Combinations (fix the size), Subsets II (skip duplicate siblings), and Permutations (track used instead of a start index) are all small edits to this same skeleton.

java.explanation: Recorded at the TOP of every call, not just at leaves — every partial path is itself a valid subset, including the empty path.

java.line: for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {
java.explanation: Loop starts at `start`, never 0 — moving forward only emits subsets in index order and prevents {1,2}/{2,1} duplicates.
The CHOOSE step: commit to including nums[i] in the current subset.

java.line: backtrack(nums, i + 1, path, results);        // explore, i+1 → each element once
java.explanation: Pass `i + 1` so later levels only see later elements — each element is used at most once (vs `i` for reuse).
The UN-CHOOSE step: pop nums[i] so the next sibling iteration starts from the correct prefix.

python.line: results.append(path[:])          # record EVERY node — each path is a subset
python.explanation: `path[:]` snapshots the list; appending `path` itself would store a reference later pops mutate. Recorded at every node, not only leaves.
Start at `start`, not 0 — the never-go-backward rule dedups {1,2} vs {2,1}.

python.line: backtrack(i + 1, path)       # explore, i+1 → each element once
python.explanation: EXPLORE from i+1 so each element appears at most once — this is what makes them subsets, not multisets.
UN-CHOOSE: pop nums[i] back off so the sibling iteration sees the original prefix.

edgeCases.behavior: Records [] at the root, then chooses 0 and records [0]. Returns [[], [0]] — confirms 0 as an element causes no truthiness issue since we never test the value.
Root records [], the single iteration records [1]. Returns [[], [1]] — the minimal 2¹ = 2 subsets.

pitfalls: Recording only at leaves (e.g. `if start == nums.length`) — yields only the single full subset instead of all 2ⁿ.
Passing `i` instead of `i + 1` — allows reuse and produces multisets like [1,1].
Appending `path` instead of `path[:]` / `new ArrayList<>(path)` — every stored subset mutates to the same final list.

approaches.name: Bitmask Enumeration (Iterative)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the clean, recursion-free alternative — 'each subset maps to an n-bit mask from 0 to 2ⁿ−1; bit i set means include nums[i]'. Great when n is small and you want to avoid a recursion stack.
hints: Each element is independently in or out — that's exactly one bit per element. How many distinct n-bit numbers are there?
Iterate an integer `mask` from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Each value of mask is one subset; the set bits tell you which elements to include.
For each mask, scan bits 0..n−1: if bit i is set (`mask & (1 << i)`), include nums[i]. No recursion, no path to copy back.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer loop runs 2ⁿ times (one per mask); the inner loop scans n bits each time, so total time is O(n · 2ⁿ). Apart from the output list, only a constant number of integer variables are used — O(1) extra space (no recursion stack).
approaches.explanation:
Every subset corresponds one-to-one with a choice of 'in or out' for each of the n elements — which is precisely an n-bit binary number. So we can skip recursion entirely: iterate `mask` over every integer from `0` to `2ⁿ − 1`, and for each one, read its bits to decide which elements to include.

**Why this is exactly equivalent to backtracking.** The recursion tree has 2ⁿ leaves-worth of subsets because each level makes a binary include/exclude decision. A bitmask collapses those decisions into the bits of a single integer: bit `i` set means 'element i is in this subset'. Counting `mask` from 0 upward enumerates every combination of those bits, hence every subset — `mask = 0` is the empty set and `mask = 2ⁿ − 1` (all bits set) is the full array.

**Why `mask & (1 << i)` is the membership test.** `(1 << i)` is an integer with only bit `i` set. ANDing it with `mask` isolates that single bit: the result is non-zero exactly when element `i` is included. Looping `i` from 0 to n−1 and including `nums[i]` whenever the test passes reconstructs the subset for that mask.

**When to prefer this over recursion.** The bitmask version has no recursion stack (O(1) extra space) and is often faster in practice due to tight integer loops and no call overhead. Its limit is that it only works while `2ⁿ` fits comfortably — for n up to ~20–30 it's fine, and this problem caps n at 10. For problems with constraints or pruning (Combination Sum, N-Queens), recursion is the natural fit; for pure power-set enumeration of small n, the bitmask is elegant.
approaches.insight: The bijection 'subset ↔ n-bit integer' is worth internalising: it turns enumeration of all subsets into a simple counting loop, and it's the basis for bitmask dynamic programming (Travelling Salesman, assignment problems) where a state IS a subset packed into an int.

dryRun.intro: mask runs 0..7 (2³ − 1). Each mask's set bits pick elements: bit 0 → nums[0]=1, bit 1 → nums[1]=2, bit 2 → nums[2]=3.

code.python:
def subsets(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    n = len(nums)
    results: list[list[int]] = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):                       # every n-bit number = one subset
        subset = [nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)]  # bit i set → include
        results.append(subset)
    return results

java.line: for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {   // every n-bit number = one subset
java.explanation: `1 << n` is 2ⁿ; iterating mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 enumerates every subset exactly once.

java.line: if ((mask & (1 << i)) != 0) {           // bit i set → include nums[i]
java.explanation: `1 << i` isolates bit i; the AND is non-zero exactly when element i is in this subset.
`subset` is freshly built each iteration, so no copy gymnastics are needed — there's no shared mutable path.

python.line: for mask in range(1 << n):                       # every n-bit number = one subset
python.explanation: `1 << n` equals 2ⁿ; counting masks enumerates the full power set.

python.line: subset = [nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)]  # bit i set → include
python.explanation: Comprehension keeps nums[i] only when bit i of mask is set — that's the membership test.
Each subset is a brand-new list, so appending it directly is safe (no aliasing).

edgeCases.behavior: n=1, masks 0 and 1. mask=0 → [], mask=1 (bit 0 set) → [0]. Value 0 is fine because we test the bit, not the value.
n=2, masks 0..3 → [], [1], [2], [1,2]. Confirms 2² = 4 subsets in mask order.

pitfalls: Writing `1 << n` as `int` when n could overflow — fine here (n ≤ 10), but for n ≥ 31 use `1L << n`.
Confusing bit index with element value — bit i selects nums[i], not the number i.
Using `mask & (1 << i)` directly as a boolean in languages where it returns the bit value — in Java compare `!= 0`; in Python it's truthy as-is.

commonMistakes: Recording subsets only at the leaves of the recursion, producing just the full array instead of all 2ⁿ subsets.
Passing `i` instead of `i + 1`, which allows element reuse and generates multisets.
Storing the live `path` reference instead of a copy, so every subset mutates to the same final list.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recording only at leaves
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only append when `start == nums.length`, you capture a single subset (the full array) and miss the empty set, singletons, and every intermediate subset. The whole point is that EVERY node is a subset.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Passing i instead of i + 1 (allows reuse)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Recursing with `i` lets the same element be chosen again at the next level, producing multisets like [1,1] and [1,1,1]. Subsets use each element at most once, so recurse with `i + 1`.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(start, len(nums)):
    path.append(nums[i])
    backtrack(i, path)        # reuse → multisets, wrong
    path.pop()
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(start, len(nums)):
    path.append(nums[i])
    backtrack(i + 1, path)    # each element at most once
    path.pop()

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Storing the live path reference
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `results.append(path)` stores the same list object; subsequent pops mutate it, so all results collapse to the same (often empty) list. Append a snapshot.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: results.append(path)        # reference to a mutating list

followupVariations.title: Subsets II
followupVariations.hint: Input has duplicates → sort first, then skip `nums[i] == nums[i-1]` when `i > start` to avoid duplicate subsets at the same level.

followupVariations.title: Combinations
followupVariations.hint: Only subsets of fixed size k → same start-index template but record when `path.size() == k` and prune branches too short to reach k.

followupVariations.title: Permutations
followupVariations.hint: Order matters and all n elements are used → drop the start index, track a used[] set, loop from 0 every level.

followupVariations.title: Combination Sum
followupVariations.hint: Add a target constraint and allow reuse → recurse with `i` (not `i+1`) and record only when remaining hits 0.

patternNote: Canonical Backtracking with a Start Index, recording at every node (choose → explore → un-choose). Recognise it whenever you must enumerate the full power set with no constraint. The 'record everywhere' twist (vs only at qualifying leaves) is what distinguishes it from Combination Sum; the same skeleton drives Subsets II, Combinations, and (with used[] instead of start) Permutations.
